question: In June 2023, a man named Nahel was killed by the French police after refusing to comply with an order. Straight away, before the legal investigations had even been concluded, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the policeman’s conduct was ‘inexplicable and inexcusable’, thus breaching the separation of powers and the presumption of innocence.

France then faced eleven days of urban riots, in which more than a thousand people were injured, including 782 law enforcement officers. 2 500 buildings were also damaged and more than 12 000 vehicles burned. A total of 50 000 people took part in the riots, with a third of them being minors and 60 % first-time offenders.

According to a report by the French Senate, the cost of material damage is around a staggering EUR 1 billion. Can the European Commission say whether it considers Macron’s statement labelling the policeman’s conduct as ‘inexplicable and inexcusable’ before any investigation had been carried out and manifestly violating the fundamental principle of the presumption of innocence to be consistent with the rule of law?
answer: It is Commission policy not to comment on public statements by politicians in the Member States. More generally, the Commission does not intervene in individual cases before national courts. The EU has since 2010 adopted six Directives establishing minimum standards in the protection of procedural rights for suspects and accused persons, aiming at a high level of fair trial rights (1).

Directive 2010/64/EU on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings; Directive 2012/13/EU on the right to information in criminal proceedings; Directive 2013/48/EU on the right of access to a lawyer in criminal proceedings and in European arrest warrant proceedings, and on the right to have a third party informed upon deprivation of liberty and to communicate with third persons and with consular authorities while deprived of liberty; Directive (EU) 2016/343 on the strengthening of certain aspects of the presumption of innocence and the right to be present at the trial; Directive (EU) 2016/800 on procedural safeguards for children who are suspects and accused in criminal proceedings; Directive (EU) 2016/1919 on legal aid for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings and for requested persons in European arrest warrant proceedings.
